transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-07-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Jordan Patel (Redwood SE), Anika Rao (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Kapella CTO), Priya Desai (Kapella Lead ML Eng), Evan Reyes (Kapella Platform Eng), Sofia Marin (Kapella Security)
Links referenced: Deck: https://redwood.link/kapella-integration-deck, Security pack: https://redwood.link/redwood-security-pack, Example repo: https://github.com/redwood/example-lc-connector

Summary:
High-level discovery about integration patterns: SDK usage, LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, gateway/proxy architecture, rate limits and quotas, and observability hooks. Kapella is evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private for latency/cost/regulatory constraints and wants concrete POC plan and pricing.

Topics: SDK compatibility, streaming + WebSocket vs HTTP, gateway auth and mTLS, rate-limiting_behavior, observability traces to Datadog, KV cache implications for sessionized chat, VPC/private deployment constraints.

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I think we've got about 50 minutes. Quick round robin intro?
[00:12] Liam (Kapella): Hi, Liam here, CTO, we run Kapella's inference infra and the thing we're trying to solve is reduce latency for our chat agent while keeping costs predictable.
[00:20] Priya (Kapella): Priya — lead ML eng. We're prototyping multi-turn retrieval augmented generation and have used Lama index and LangChain in experiments.
[00:32] Jordan (Redwood SE): Jordan — I'll be the SE pair today, I'll dig into the connector details and perf.
[00:38] Sofia (Kapella Security): Sofia — security architect, I'll surface the compliance needs.
[00:42] Anika (Redwood SE): Anika — I'll follow up on observability hooks and example configs.
[00:45] Evan (Kapella Platform): Evan — platform eng, curious about proxy/gateway patterns and quotas.
[00:50] Maya: Great. Quick agenda: SDKs and LangChain/LlamaIndex support, proxy/gateway options (we've seen people do sidecar vs central gateway), quotas/ratelimiting and token accounting, and observability integrations. Then agree next steps. Sound good?
[00:59] Liam: Yep.

[01:06] Jordan: To start, on SDKs — Redwood has official SDKs in Python/Node/Go, and we also publish connectors for LangChain and a reference for LlamaIndex. The LangChain connector supports the chains and agents pattern; the LlamaIndex repo is a light adapter — not perfect but something you can fork.
[01:23] Priya: Do you have a handed sample for how the streaming token-level responses map into LangChain streams? Last time we had trouble with partial tokens and prompts getting duplicated.
[01:33] Jordan: Yes, we have an example — see the example repo link — but important note: streaming can be via server-sent events (SSE) or websocket depending on your stack. The Node SDK exposes both, Python SDK uses SSE by default but you can opt into a websocket client.
[01:50] Priya: Ok. In our infra we prefer websocket because we have persistent connections from the gateway.
[01:56] Jordan: Websocket is supported on Redwood Hosted and Dedicated. For Private (on-prem) the gateway can be configured to allow ws, but you'll need to open the appropriate ports in the VPC.

[02:10] Evan: About gateway patterns — we're evaluating two: 1) a centralized API gateway that proxies all app traffic to Redwood hosted endpoints, or 2) a sidecar pattern where each service talks directly to Redwood via SDK. Pros/cons?
[02:23] Anika: Central gateway gives you centralized quotas, single point to add caching and prefix caching, and easier observability. Sidecar reduces hop count for chat and can do local cache for KV which helps latency. But sidecars mean you need consistent SDK versions everywhere.
[02:39] Liam: For us, any extra hop is painful — our latency budget is 150ms tail for user-facing chat. How much overhead does the gateway add?
[02:46] Jordan: Typically 10–30ms per hop if proxy is lightweight, more if you're doing heavy transformations. The bigger factor is whether you rely on batching and KV cache; Redwood's continuous batching is per-model worker so if you route via a central gateway that shards requests nicely you can gain throughput efficiency.

[03:05] Priya: On KV cache — we saw notes about prefix caching for RAG sessions. If we put caching in the gateway, does it conflict with Redwood's own KV cache?
[03:13] Jordan: Good question. Redwood's runtime will do KV cache at the model-serving layer (that's the KV cache for token keys). Application-level cache in the gateway should be session/prefix caching (e.g., doc-level embeddings, rerank results). They complement each other. But make sure TTLs align; you don't want the gateway to serve stale embeddings while the model expects newer context.

[03:33] [crosstalk]
[03:36] Sofia: Security: for Dedicated or Private we need KMS integration, HSM if possible, and audit logs. Do you support customer-managed keys and exportable audit trails?
[03:45] Maya: Yes — Private supports customer KMS (AWS KMS and others via KMS providers). Dedicated also supports bring-your-own-key for enterprise. Audit logs are available through the Console and we can stream to your SIEM (Splunk/Datadog) or S3.
[03:58] Sofia: And the retention window?
[04:01] Anika: By default 90 days in the console; longer via enterprise add-on. We'll send the security pack that lists options.

[04:12] Liam: On-hosted vs dedicated: what are the tradeoffs for throughput/cost? We might start Hosted to iterate, then lock in Dedicated for predictable costs. Any gotchas on migrating models/rollouts between modes?
[04:24] Jordan: Movement is generally straightforward — model versions and routing policies are abstracted in the control plane. You can pin a model version in Dedicated or have fallback to hosted variants. The main cost/tradeoff is cold-starts and reserved capacity planning — Dedicated gives you guaranteed GPUs and lower per-token cost at scale, Hosted is more flexible but has variable latency under heavy load.

[04:48] Priya: Rate limiting — we need per-tenant quotas with burst behavior. Can Redwood enforce per-API-key rate limits and per-route quotas?
[04:57] Maya: Yes. Redwood supports token and request-level quotas, per-API-key and per-route. You can define burst windows and token budgets; we expose quota errors with a specific HTTP response so your gateway can implement backoffs.

[05:12] Evan: Does the SDK surface error metadata for quota usage so we can build client-side throttling?
[05:18] Jordan: Yes — the SDK surfaces headers and structured error fields: remaining tokens, quota-reset, and suggested-retry-after. Small caveat: in older SDK versions some of the headers had slightly different names — update to latest.

[05:34] Priya: Observability — we use Datadog for traces and Prometheus for infra metrics. How do we hook Redwood traces into Datadog?
[05:43] Anika: Redwood Console can emit traces via OTLP to your Datadog agent. We also provide span-level hooks that include model_id, prompt_hash, token_count, and latency. For infra metrics you can pull via Prometheus exporter or stream to your metrics ingest.

[05:58] Liam: Can we get token-level cost breakdown per request in our tracing so a product owner can see cost per conversation?
[06:05] Anika: Yes — token-level breakdowns are included in the trace attributes. We'll show an example in the repo.

[06:14] [longer pause — note: discussion about sample workload sizing]
[06:40] Jordan: For the POC we recommend a small benchmark: 1) 90-second simulated chat sessions with avg 4 turns, 2) 10k simulated users over 1 hour to test throughput, 3) tail latency SLO checks. We'll provide a load harness or you can use k6/JMeter.

[07:00] Priya: About LlamaIndex — last time we tried the LlamaIndex adapter it mangled schema when using structured output. Any improvements?
[07:08] Jordan: We've updated the reference adapter to better preserve structured output. There's still some mapping between LlamaIndex's index nodes and Redwood's streaming tokenization; we'll send a patched example.

[07:20] Sofia: Compliance checklist — does Redwood have SOC2 type II and ISO 27001? Also EEA data residency options?
[07:28] Maya: Redwood has SOC2 reports and ISO certification in our enterprise pack; EEA regions are supported in hosted with data residency options and Dedicated/Private gives you full control of region. We'll attach the certs in the security pack link.

[07:40] Evan: For Private deployments, what does the control plane look like? Is there an air-gapped option?
[07:47] Jordan: Private has two modes: connected private (control plane in Redwood but data path in your VPC) and fully air-gapped on-prem package. Air-gapped requires additional ops work — we have a deployment checklist and an ops-runbook we'll share.

[08:02] Liam: Let's talk about a common gotcha — model fallbacks. If Dedicated capacity is saturated, will requests automatically failover to hosted variants?
[08:12] Anika: You can configure smart routing policies: failover to a hosted-compatible model, or queue with a retry/backoff. We can set cost-based routing too so non-critical paths hit cheaper quantized variants.

[08:25] Priya: Any limits on model quantization support? We use a quantized 4-bit for cost savings — will that degrade our embeddings or cause rerank drift?
[08:35] Jordan: Some quantization profiles change token logits slightly. We offer recommendations in Redwood Optimize — for embeddings we often recommend higher-precision quant profiles. We'll include model-specific guidance in the POC doc.

[08:50] [noise, someone typing]

[09:00] Maya: Ok to surface a few pragmatic POC next steps: 1) Redwood sends Dedicated worksheet and pricing, 2) Jordan sends LangChain and LlamaIndex sample repo + an example websocket client, 3) Kapella to provide a small sanitized dataset and define success criteria for latency and cost.
[09:18] Liam: Sounds good. Our success criteria: 95th perc latency < 150ms, per-conversation cost <$0.10, and SOC2 alignment for logs.
[09:29] Maya: Great — we'll align on those.

[09:35] Priya: One last question: do you have any recommended proxy libs or gateway configs? We're using Envoy and Kong.
[09:42] Jordan: Envoy works great — we have a sample envoy filter to pass through streaming and preserve SSE headers. Kong is fine too but might need plugin work for the streaming edge cases. We'll share the envoy snippet.

[09:56] Sofia: For the audit logs — can we get field-level redaction before logs leave our VPC?
[10:02] Anika: With Private and Dedicated you can enable field-level redaction in the agent configuration. We'll include the config example in the security pack.

[10:12] [summary and recap from Maya]
[10:14] Maya: Quick recap — we'll send pricing and security docs, SE to send connector examples and envoy snippet, Kapella to send dataset and compliance questionnaire. We'll schedule the POC benchmark session for the week of 2026-07-27. Any blockers?
[10:29] Liam: No blockers, just need the pricing sooner if possible.
[10:33] Maya: We'll prioritize. Thanks everyone.
[10:36] [meeting ends]

Notes about transcription: some brand names were auto-corrected (LlamaIndex -> Lama index in earlier drafts), occasional timestamp drift in the auto transcript.
